Rust's test story is unusually good: tests live in the same file, they are just functions, and the doc examples in your comments are tests too.

Unit tests

#[cfg(test)] means the module is only compiled for cargo test, so it costs nothing in release builds. use super::* gives access to the parent module's items — including private ones, which is why unit tests can test internals.

Assertions

Integration tests

tests/ is a separate crate. It can only use your public API — which is exactly the check you want for a library.

Shared helpers

Any .rs file directly in tests/ becomes a test binary; a subdirectory does not.

Async tests

Doc tests

Doc tests are why Rust's documentation is trustworthy: every example on docs.rs was executed on the author's machine.

Gotcha: doc tests link against your crate as an external user would, so they can only see public items. And they are slow to compile in bulk — cargo test --lib skips them when you are iterating fast.

Test organisation that scales

Rule: unit tests next to the code (they test internals), integration tests in tests/ (they test the API), end-to-end tests as a separate crate or a shell script against a running service.

Test doubles

Hand-written traits (preferred)

Time, randomness, and I/O are the three things worth abstracting. Everything else can usually be tested directly.

mockall

Property-based testing with proptest

Instead of one example, generate hundreds and shrink failures to a minimal case.

The value is in the shrunk counter-example: instead of [1, 2, 3] you get the exact minimal input that breaks the invariant.

Snapshot testing with insta

First run writes .snap.new files; cargo insta review shows a diff and lets you accept. Ideal for CLI output, HTML rendering, and JSON API responses.

Benchmarking with criterion

black_box stops the optimiser from constant-folding your benchmark into nothing. Criterion does statistical analysis, detects regressions, and writes HTML reports with plots to target/criterion/.

Gotcha: benchmarking a debug build measures nothing useful. Criterion uses the bench profile (release-like) automatically — but cargo run does not.

Running tests fast: cargo-nextest

Nextest runs each test in its own process (so a segfault or a leaked global does not poison the suite), parallelises better than cargo test, and has a cleaner output format. On large suites it is 2–5× faster.

Coverage

Do not chase 100%. Aim for coverage of decision points — every match arm, every Err path — not every line.

A worked example: testing an HTTP handler

oneshot runs the router without binding a port. That is the fastest and most reliable way to test HTTP handlers.

CI gate

Exercises

  1. Add a unit test module to a module with a private helper, and assert on the private function directly.
  2. Write an integration test that uses only the public API, then make the function private and confirm it fails to compile.
  3. Write a doc test that is should_panic and one that is compile_fail.
  4. Introduce a Clock trait, implement SystemClock and FixedClock, and test a function that uses it.
  5. Write a proptest for fn reverse(s: &str) -> String asserting reverse(reverse(s)) == s.
  6. Benchmark two implementations of the same string parser with criterion and report the ratio.
